lohr-brick-2017-literary-digest.title: Roosevelt predicted to win: Revisiting the 1936 Literary Digest poll

verified.note: Crossref record matched. Full text read (PDF copy): about 10 million ballots sent, almost 2.4 million returned (24 percent response rate); final Literary Digest forecast Landon 54 percent and 370 electoral votes; Roosevelt won more than 60 percent and 523 electoral votes; the frame came mainly from telephone directories and automobile registration lists; Gallup (1938) blamed the frame, Bryson (1976) and Squire (1988) stressed nonresponse. Secondary literature often gives 57 percent for Landon; the lesson uses the figure from this article.

squire-1988-literary-digest.title: Why the 1936 Literary Digest poll failed

verified.note: Crossref record and abstract matched (uses a 1937 Gallup survey that asked about participation in the Digest poll; sample and response were both biased; had everybody responded the magazine would still have named Roosevelt). Page range 125-133 as given in the reference list of Lohr & Brick 2017, which also summarises Squire's argument. Full text not read.

Crossref record matched (start page 91 only; end page 92 as commonly cited, not independently confirmed - the lesson does not cite pages). The article itself was not opened (paywalled). Its allow/forbid result (21 percent vs 39 percent favouring free speech; equivalently 75 vs 54 percent among those with an opinion) is taken from Bradburn 2000 (a conference paper, read in full) and Frankovic 2007 (CBS News); the two sources are consistent with each other.

verified.note: PDF read in full text. The author is listed as Norman M. Bradburn, National Science Foundation, in the paper's header. Used only for the Rugg (1941) allow/forbid result (21% vs 39%).

verified.note: Crossref record and AEA abstract matched; full text read (PDF copy): Prince William County, Virginia; 3,347 households that said they took neither paper, randomly assigned to a free ten-week subscription to the Washington Post, to the Washington Times, or to a control group; baseline survey in September 2005, follow-up survey after the November 2005 gubernatorial election (1,081 re-interviewed), plus administrative voter records; the paper calls the Times conservative and the Post more liberal. verified.note: Crossref record matched (English DOI 10.1590/1809-58442023118en; the Portuguese original has DOI ...118pt). English PDF read (Redalyc): the Columbia group, funded by the Rockefeller Foundation and linked to the Bureau of Applied Social Research, went to Erie County, Ohio; the question was why people vote as they do; the design was six months of research from May 1940 to just after the election, with individual open-ended interviews repeated every month with a representative group of 600 people; the main finding stressed personal relationships and opinion leaders. The page's own statement that the book was 'originally published in 1948' conflicts with 1944 in Open Library and Sills 1987, so no publication year of the original is taken from it.
